member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2RenderGroups
member.summary: Which of the frame's sixteen queues each kind of object is drawn in.

remarks.para: The frame has no hardcoded pass order; it has queues. World_Draw (igi2ed 0x417F50) draws nothing itself — it initialises sixteen call queues, walks the world cube tree so the traversal enqueues each visible object, and then QCube_CallHandlers (0x4171B0) empties them 0 to 15, flushing shadow volumes after each and bracketing the lot with QTask events 17 and 18. The queue an object goes in is DynCubeObj_s::iRenderGroup, and the enqueue is one line (0x41784F): CallQueue_QueueEvent(8 * group + &QCube_atCallQueues, object, 5, …). Event five is the draw event, which is why terrain, water, forest and the sky all reach the screen through their own *_EnterHandler and nothing calls those directly.

The numbers below are read out of the create handlers rather than measured from level data, because most of them are the engine's choice and not an author's. A level may override its rigid objects — I.G.I. 2 registers RenderGroup as a level parameter and all 24 levels use it — but what it mostly ships is the value the engine would have picked anyway.

A caution about offsets. The dedicated server's symbols put iRenderGroup at 0x6C of a 112-byte DynCubeObj_s; the editor's code reads it at 124. Both are right — the editor's layout is the server's plus sixteen bytes, which the list link confirms independently (server ptNext at 0x60, editor at 0x70, the +112 World_Draw itself chains by). The two binaries' structures are not interchangeable, and the only one with type information is the one without a renderer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2RenderGroups.Count
member.summary: How many queues the frame has.
member.remarks: Sixteen, and arithmetic rather than a guess: the flush calls CallQueue_CallHandlers(8 * i + 0x788700), and 0x788700 to 0x788780 is exactly sixteen queues of eight bytes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2RenderGroups.Sky

member.remarks: Nought, the first queue emptied — and registered through World_RegisterManualObj rather than into the cube tree, so it is enqueued before the traversal runs at all. Both halves say the same thing: a backdrop is drawn before everything, which is what lets it be drawn with no depth.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2RotateAttachments
member.summary: The parts of I.G.I. 2's objects that turn on the spot.

remarks.para: A RotateAttachment places nothing. It names a part that some other task's model already carries — by model name and, where an object has several of them, by which one — and gives it three rotation speeds. RotateAttachment_UpdateInternalDataHandler (igi2ed 0x671B50) walks UP from the task to the first object-derived ancestor, then along that object's attachment list for the Nth entry whose model matches, and keeps a reference to it. That is the whole of its placement work: the geometry was already there.

What it does every tick is RotateAttachment_RunHandler (0x671730): build a rotation from the three speeds as Euler angles, multiply the part's LOCAL orientation by it, re-orthonormalise, and re-run the attachment update so the world transform follows. So the speeds are radians per tick, not per second — the handler never looks at elapsed time.

Which means the port needs no local orientations. The world orientation of a part is its parent's times its local one, and only the local one turns, so the world orientation after t ticks is simply the authored world orientation times the same power. The placement the walk already produced is the starting point, and nothing has to be recomposed up the tree.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SceneAtmosphere
member.summary: The air a level is played in: what colour the distance goes, how quickly it gets there, and the flat light everything sits in. Read from I.G.I. 2's GlobalLight task.

remarks.para: This is the sequel's whole atmosphere, and the port had none of it. GlobalLightQTask_DrawCallback (igi2ed 0x6534E0) is four calls long and does all of it once a frame:
remarks.code: DrawTerrainMesh_SetAmbientColor(globalLight + 108) // tObjectAmbientColor vDensity = *(float *)(globalLight + 132) * 0.0005 // vObjectFogDensity DrawTerrainMesh_SetFog(globalLight + 120, vDensity) // tObjectFogColor Sky_SetColor(globalLight + 56)
remarks.para: Those three offsets are twelve bytes apart and then four, which is exactly GlobalLightCategory_t as the dedicated server's own type information lays it out — tObjectAmbientColor, tObjectFogColor, vObjectFogDensity — so the arithmetic names itself.

The fog is on everything. Every render state block in the game enables it against this one colour: the ground (TerrainRender_SetGenericState, 0x66BAD0), the foliage (ForestRender_SetGenericState_AlphaTestFoliage, 0x57C770), the water and the objects. TerrainRender_CalculateRenderVertex (0x66A740) writes exp(-density * distance) into the fourth float of every terrain vertex, and TerrainRender_SetVertexShaderConstants (0x667D20) hands the shader the view-space depth row scaled by the same density. It is a plain exponential haze, per vertex, in front of the whole world.

Which is why a night level reads as night. location1/level1 authors a fog colour of (0, 0.162, 0.287) — a deep blue — over an ambient of (0.058, 0.100, 0.180). Without the haze the port drew every surface at its own unfogged colour against a black sky, so the distance stayed as contrasty as the foreground and nothing took the night's cast.

This is the sequel's alone. Project I.G.I. has no GlobalLight task and no fog here, and nothing in this type is reachable from its title — see ITitlePresentationProvider.ReadAtmosphere, which only this game answers.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SceneAtmosphere.AuthoredDensityScale
member.summary: What the authored density is multiplied by on its way to a per-metre extinction.

remarks.para: GlobalLightQTask_DrawCallback writes vObjectFogDensity * 0.0005, and that number is per DIRECT3D UNIT, not per metre. Direct3D_New (igi2ed 0x55AE63) sets Direct3D_vScale to 0.001 — a Direct3D unit is a thousand engine units, about a quarter of a metre — and every distance the fog is evaluated over is scaled by it: Direct3DRender_SetFogParameters (0x5681E0) multiplies an object's view depth by vScale before the density, and TerrainRender_SetVertexShaderConstants (0x667D20) builds the matrix TerrainRender_CalculateRenderVertex (0x66A740) takes its depth from with vScale on its diagonal. A metre is 4.096 of those units, so the per-metre extinction is 0.0005 × 4.096.

location1/level1's authored 0.85 is therefore 1.74e-3 per metre — a haze that halves what it is looking through every four hundred metres — and not the 4.25e-4 this constant first read, which left every tank, tree and hill a quarter as hazed as the original draws them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SectorGraph
member.summary: The sector objects an I.G.I. 2 level places, each a shell and its rooms, and which of them a portal can lead to.

remarks.para: Only a Building is a sector object. SectorObject derives from Sector (SectorObject_Open), and of every task type the client registers only Building derives from SectorObject (building.c). Its model is its shell, a sector whose portals are the building's openings to the outside.

Its rooms are its model's attach objects that are sectors. SectorObject_SetModel gives the object two containers, ptMagicObjContainer and ptSectorContainer, and SectorObject_CreateAttachObjects makes every attach point of the shell's model an object, moving each one derived from Sector into the second. The port reads the same thing the collision world does: an attach point the magic table does not hold whose model carries portals. Across the 24 shipped levels that is 375 rooms in 230 of the 491 buildings.

Linkage is by portal slot within one building. SectorObject_TraverseSector (igi2.exe 0x588830), having found a portal visible, offers the building being drawn -- SectorObject_ptActiveSectorObject -- and then every child of its ptSectorContainer, and admits each with a portal whose equals the slot just stepped through. A room's doorway onto the street and the shell's opening in the same place carry the same number; nothing pairs them in space. No portal leads from one building into another.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SectorLocator
member.summary: Which room of which building a point stands in: QCube_eGetSectorQTaskEvent, which every sector object answers with SectorObject_GetSectorHandler (e/3/sectorobject.c).

remarks.para: A building asks each of its rooms in turn: two lines from the point, one straight down and one straight up, each twice the building's registered radius long, traced against that room alone with its portals counted as surfaces. The point is in the room when both strike it; of every room so placed, in every building near the point, the nearest strike wins.

Rooms, not shells. The shell is the building's outside and is never answered. A point inside a building that carries no room is in no sector -- which is what the original's cull reads: such a building leaves its surroundings drawn.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SectorPortals
member.summary: Which of each sector's portals are open, Sector_s.atPortalStatus: a byte a portal, which the doors standing in them count up and down and the sector walk reads.

remarks.para: Every sector starts with all sixty-four bytes at one (memset(..., 1, 0x40) in the sector object's create). A door linked to a portal writes its own state there as it attaches and then adds one as it is told to open and takes one away, not below nought, as it comes to rest shut (Door_RunHandler). Two doors in one portal therefore keep it open until both are shut.

Sector_IsPortalVisible is the only reader: a portal whose byte is nought is not looked through. So the state decides what the sector walk reaches and nothing else -- no line, no sound, no soldier reads it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SectorVisibility
member.summary: I.G.I. 2's sector cull, decided once a frame from the eye: which buildings, rooms, objects and soldiers are drawn, whether the outside is, and through what part of the screen.

remarks.para: Where the camera stands decides the frame. ViewportQTask_DrawHandler asks which room the camera is in (ViewPortQTask_FindSector, without tolerance), and World_Draw hands the answer to everything it draws:

list.item: The building the camera stands in is walked from its room through the whole screen (SectorObject_EnterHandler). Its shell is drawn only if the walk reaches it, which it does through a portal of the room that shares a slot with one of the shell's -- the outside is then seen, through the rectangles that reached the shell (SectorObject_DrawSector sets QCube_isDrawOutside and Clipping_tClipData.tClipWindows).

Until then nothing outside is drawn: the terrain and the forests test QCube_isDrawOutside, every other building returns without a request, and every rigid mesh standing in no room returns from Direct3DRender_DrawRigidMesh -- a door and a conveyor belt excepted. Once it is, another building is walked from its shell through each of those rectangles, a mesh outside is drawn if its sphere falls in one of them, and the terrain and the forests are clipped to the rectangle enclosing them all (Clipping_SetupClippingPlanes's enclosing frustum, which only they read).
With the camera in no room, every building is walked from its shell through the whole screen; its rooms are drawn only if reached.

An interior object standing in a room is drawn only while that room is reached, and only if its sphere falls in one of the rectangles the room was reached through. A soldier is decided the same way by the room its nodes place it in ().

remarks.para: What is not reproduced. A building whose level of detail is -1 is not skipped; the renderer's own distance handling stands in for it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SmokeTask
member.summary: A plume of smoke, steam or fire, I.G.I. 2's Smoke (smoke.c): a particle system that sprays particles in a cone from its place, at a rate its generate factor sets, and that may burn the player standing in it.

remarks.para: Smoke_UpdateInternalDataHandler makes its particle system: its sprite by index (nought the fireball, which also burns at half a point a second within a metre unless told otherwise; one blood; two the second smoke; above, the first), its fade mode's transparency, a fall of its gravity factor, its colour, size and size delta, and a view cutoff; its direction is the third column of its alpha-and-gamma turn.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SplineObject
member.summary: A SplineObj and its waypoints, read into the segments that are drawn between them.

remarks.para: A spline is the one thing in an I.G.I. 2 level whose geometry is not declared anywhere. The waypoints are declared; the segments between them are made at load, one per waypoint after the first, each bending that waypoint's Segment Model along the curve from the waypoint before it. 678 of the corpus's 713 waypoints carry one, and they are the roads, pipe runs, fences and cable trays that the levels are threaded with.

Read as the settled state, not as a replay. The original arrives here through SplineObjWaypoint_UpdateInternalDataHandler (igi2ed 0x6417C0), which fires once per waypoint on load and then a second time for the whole spline from SplineObj_UpdateInternalDataAfterLoadHandler (0x6436C0). Each firing recomputes the waypoint's own orientation and then rebuilds the segments on either side of it. What it converges to is what this computes directly, in one pass over the waypoints, which is the same answer without the event ordering.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SplinePath
member.summary: A whole spline, end to end, as something that can be walked by distance.

remarks.para: The segments drawn between waypoints are also the track a Train rides. A train carries no position: it names a spline and a distance along it, and everything else follows from walking the curve. SplineObj_GetPosAndMatrix (igi2ed 0x63FA10) is that walk, and this is its position half — a train asks for no matrix, passing null for it, and builds each carriage's facing from the two points the carriage spans.

A carriage is rigid and the track is not straight. Which is why stepping back from the locomotive is not simply subtracting arc length. The original walks areas until it finds the pair whose ends straddle the wanted STRAIGHT-LINE distance, then solves the triangle they make with the point it is stepping from: a cosine rule for the angle at the near frame, a sine rule for where along that area the chord comes out right. A train on a curve is shorter along the track than it is long.

member.remarks: The original's own threshold, in radians, from 0x63FA10.

member.summary: Solves where along one area a point sits at a given straight-line distance from somewhere else.
member.param: The squared distance from the anchor to the area's first frame.
The squared distance from the anchor to the area's second frame.
The straight-line distance wanted, as a positive length.
Whether the walk arrived from the far end, which is what stepping BACK down the spline does. It decides which end the sine rule measures from, and therefore which way round the answer is.
member.returns: The fraction along the area, from its first frame to its second.

The cosine rule gives the angle the area leaves that end at; the sine rule then gives how far along the area the answer lies. Where the triangle collapses — anchor, end and answer in a line — the original interpolates the two end distances instead, and does so from the FIRST frame either way round.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2SplineSweep
member.summary: A model bent along the curve between two spline waypoints — the sequel's SplineObjSegment.

remarks.para: The segment is not a placement. Nothing in the level data declares one. A SplineObjWaypoint declares a Segment Model, and SplineObjWaypoint_UpdateInternalDataHandler (igi2ed 0x6417C0) hands it to SplineObjSegment_Update (0x611FB0) together with the PREVIOUS waypoint — so the segment spans from the waypoint before it to the waypoint that owns it, and the first waypoint of a spline owns none.

How the curve is built. Three cubic Hermite channels, one per axis, through the two endpoints, with each end's tangent taken from the first column of that waypoint's orientation and scaled by the straight-line distance between them (Hermite64_Init, 0x66FDF0). The segment is then sampled at areas + 1 evenly spaced parameters. At the ends the waypoints' own orientations are used verbatim; in between, the frame is Real32x9_Create(alpha, beta, gamma) where beta and gamma come from the curve's tangent there (Real32x3_GetAngles, 0x604FA0) and alpha is interpolated between the two ends' own alphas, each unwrapped so the roll takes the short way round.

How the model is bent. Direct3DRender_ProcessVerticesSplineRigid (0x568380) consumes the model's local X as position ALONG the curve: it is rescaled from the model's own X extent onto [0, areas], which picks a pair of neighbouring frames and a fraction between them. The vertex is then placed by each of the two frames — its Y and Z read as offsets in that frame's cross-section — and the two results are mixed by the fraction. Normals take the lower frame's rotation whole. So the model tiles once along the segment and rolls with it.
A linear segment skips all of that: one frame, and a single matrix whose first column is the chord itself divided by the model's X extent, so the model is simply stretched from end to end.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainHeightPyramid
member.summary: The lowest and highest height over every power-of-two block of a tile.

remarks.para: TerrainMap_AllocateMinMaxHeightMipMaps (igi2ed 0x6296B0) allocates floor(log2(max(nWidth, nHeight))) + 1 levels and 8 * nWidth * nHeight bytes for the finest — two floats a sample, a minimum and a maximum — halving both extents each level up. The original also refuses the pyramid for its two finest levels and falls back to a per-level maximum deviation (TerrainMap_t::avDeltaZ, reached at 0x66AF9E); this uses the pyramid all the way down, which is strictly tighter and costs nothing once the pyramid exists.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainLod
member.summary: The quadtree I.G.I. 2 tessellates a terrain tile with: how finely a square is subdivided given where it is being looked at from, and how a newly split vertex is faded in.

remarks.para: Read from TerrainRender_Draw (igi2ed 0x668680), which is one 8,224-byte function with an explicit stack — TerrainRender_atDrawSquareStack, 5,000 TerrainRenderStackSquare_t entries — rather than recursion. The struct names come from the dedicated server's own type information, which is what makes the stack layout legible: { nX, nY, nSize, iMipMap, iTerrainMap, nShift, aiVertex[4], aiEdge[4] }.

A square has five edges, not four. The perimeter (0,1) (1,2) (2,3) (3,0) and the diagonal (1,3), whose midpoint is the square's centre — the corner order is (0,0) (1,0) (1,1) (0,1), set up at 0x66869D, and the pairs are the table built at 0x668E3D. Each of the five is tested independently, and if any one of them splits the whole square is subdivided into four children (0x66937A: the traversal draws a leaf only when none of the five did).

The split decision is cached on the shared edge, which is what makes the mesh crack-free. TerrainRenderEdge_t::eSplitStatus carries bit 0 for "split" and bit 1 for "did not" (0x669359, 0x66935E), and a square that finds an edge already decided takes the answer rather than re-deriving it (0x668F94). So two squares sharing an edge always agree. An edge that did not split still gets a split vertex — at morph zero, which the cosine blend below puts exactly on the straight line between its parents, so the extra vertex is invisible and the seam is closed by construction rather than by a stitching pass.
The test itself (0x668FD3 to 0x669328), for an edge from a to b with the eye at the origin:

item.description: find the point on the segment nearest the eye — t = clamp(-dot(a, b - a) / |b - a|², 0, 1) — and take d², its squared distance. Not the midpoint and not either end: an edge running away from the viewer is judged by whichever part of it is closest.
measure the roughness the edge hides: |mean(a.z, b.z) - height(midpoint)| over the square's width in world units, which is zero where the midpoint falls outside the height map.
refuse the split outright if the edge is steeper than to one in both horizontal axes.
split when |b - a|² > D²d² and |b - a|² > , where D = vDetail / (1 + 0.5 * roughness * vAdapt).
record how far past the threshold it went, ((|b - a|² / D²d²) - 1) * vMorphSpeed clamped to one, as the edge's morph fraction.

remarks.para: The root square is one sample larger than the tile. It spans sample indices 0..n inclusive with n = max(width, height), so it is a clean power of two and the quadtree halves evenly. The row and column at n lie outside the height map and the original extrapolates them linearly — 0x668B08 reads 3h[w-1,h-1] - h[w-2,h-1] - h[w-1,h-2] at the far corner, 2h[w-1,y] - h[w-2,y] and 2h[x,h-1] - h[x,h-2] along the two far edges. Reproduced here, which is why the tessellated tile reaches half a texel further than 's does.

What is not reproduced. The original runs one quadtree over the whole terrain and descends into a neighbouring tile through TerrainContext_t::aapiSubmap, a per-square map index that lets a square change which height map it is reading (0x668CBF). This builds one quadtree per tile and stops each one where the finer tile begins, which decides from the same measurements Terrain_UpdateSubmaps takes. The two agree on which ground each tile owns; where they differ is the seam between them, which the original's shared-edge cache closes and separate trees cannot. Also absent: TerrainRender_DrawGlitchPolyRecursive (0x66A930), the original's repair for the T-junction a coarse square leaves against a finer neighbour that subdivided after it was drawn.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainLodSettings
member.summary: The two numbers a level authors to control how finely its ground is tessellated.
member.param: Terrain_t::vDetail. The angular size an edge has to reach before it is worth splitting: an edge splits when its length over its distance to the eye exceeds this, so a larger value means a coarser ground.
Terrain_t::vAdapt. How much local roughness lowers that threshold — the edge test divides by 1 + 0.5 * roughness * Adaption, so a bumpy patch is refined sooner than a flat one at the same distance.

remarks.para: Both are read straight out of TerrainRender_Draw (igi2ed 0x6691D3), which is the only place either is consulted:
remarks.code: fmul [ctx+1Ch] ; roughness * vAdapt fmul 0.5 fadd 1.0 fdivr [ctx+24h] ; vDetail / (1 + 0.5 * roughness * vAdapt)
remarks.para: ctx+0x1C and ctx+0x24 are TerrainContext_t::vAdapt and ::vDetail, named by the dedicated server's own type information, and the level copies them from the Terrain task's Adaption and Detail parameters.

member.summary: Gets how far a vertex has travelled from its parents' midpoint toward its own height.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainPass.BaseIndices
member.summary: Gets the triangles this pass draws as the ground's opaque base.

remarks.para: The ground has to be opaque somewhere, and the material passes on their own never are. They blend SRCALPHA onto ONE — every pass ADDS — so a ground built only from them cannot hide what is behind it or what was drawn before it. The frame draws the world's objects before the terrain (walls are the best occluders, and early-Z then rejects the ground behind them), so an additive-only ground left every crate and fence it should have buried showing through the hillside, and let the far side of a valley show through the near side.

So each triangle is written ONCE, opaquely and with depth, by the lowest-numbered pass that covers it, and every other pass that covers it adds its share on top with depth test only. The sum is unchanged — the fragment shader scales albedo by the pass's share whatever the blend, and the shares still sum to one — but the ground now owns its pixels.

This is the arrangement I.G.I. 1's own terrain uses in this port (TerrainRenderer draws its base layer Opaque and its overlays Additive), and it is what the original's render state asks for: TerrainRender_SetGenericState (igi2ed 0x66BAD0) writes D3DRS_ZWRITEENABLE = 1 and D3DRS_ZFUNC = D3DCMP_LESSEQUAL, so the ground writes depth and its own later passes still pass the test at equal depth.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainPass.OverlayIndices
member.summary: Gets the triangles this pass adds on top of a base another pass has written.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainMesh
member.summary: A terrain tile as geometry: one vertex grid, and one pass per material painted on it.

remarks.para: A triangle belongs to every material that appears at any of its corners. Not to a majority, and not to a per-face id — TerrainRender_DrawFace (igi2ed 0x66AAB0) walks the materials the tile uses and emits the triangle into each one whose bit is set in mask[v0] | mask[v1] | mask[v2]. The passes then blend, each contributing where its own corners are, which is what makes one material fade into the next across a shared edge.

The per-vertex bits are set by TerrainRender_CalculateRenderVertex (0x66A740), which also keeps the weight this exposes: a vertex contributes fully to its own material's pass and nothing to another's.

The passes are additive, weighted by source alpha, and their order does not matter. TerrainRender_SetBlendState (igi2ed 0x66BCB0) is three calls — ALPHABLENDENABLE = 1, SRCBLEND = SRCALPHA, DESTBLEND = ONE — so each pass adds texture * diffuse * weight onto the frame. The weights at a sample sum to one, which turns the accumulation into a weighted average without needing the passes sorted. That is why may be emitted in any order at all.
It also means a sample no pass covers contributes nothing rather than falling back to a default — see .

This is the tile at full detail, and that is a deliberate difference. The original draws through a quadtree whose tessellation varies with distance, morphing a vertex toward the midpoint of its two parents as a level of detail fades — a cosine blend applied to Z alone. Reproducing that needs the quadtree and a camera; reproducing the geometry does not, and a renderer can draw this correctly today and refine later. What is not approximated is the material split above, because that changes which pixels are which material rather than how many triangles carry them.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainMesh.GroundIndices
member.summary: Gets every triangle the ground draws, whatever material -- if any -- covers it.

remarks.para: The terrain map's own pass, and the original issues it unconditionally. TerrainRender_DrawFace (igi2ed 0x66AAB0) walks the tile's material buffers and issues the face into each one whose bit is set in mask[v0] | mask[v1] | mask[v2] -- and then, AFTER that loop and outside it, issues the same face once more into AllocateRenderChunk(iTerrainMap, 0, 3). Nothing about a material guards that second issue. The only thing that can stop a face going anywhere is the discard AND of its three corners, which is tested before either.

Which matters for the faces no material covers. A sample painted with a material its level later deleted is in no buffer, so a face whose three corners are all such samples takes no material pass -- and this port, which drew its pass 3 by walking the material passes, therefore drew it NOWHERE. That is a hole in the ground with the sky behind it, and there are 758 samples across the corpus that can open one.

So the pass is collected as the original collects it, and the ground's bake is drawn from here rather than from the material passes' base lists. The two agree everywhere a material exists, which is everywhere but those 758.

member.summary: Gets the texture coordinate a pass samples at one world position.
member.param: The material's texture scale, in metres per repeat.

The material's eMappingStyle, which picks one of three vertex shaders (TerrainRender_anVertexShader): nought lays the textures along X and Y, one along X and Z, two along Y and Z -- the last two for cliffs, which a flat projection stretches.
member.remarks: A world-space planar projection, and the same one for both texture stages. TerrainRender_SetMaterialTextures (igi2ed 0x667330) uploads 1 / (vScale * 4096) into vertex-shader constants 11 and 12 with U and V set alike, and the shader multiplies the world position by it. So the scale is metres per repeat, the terrain's texturing does not follow the tile's own grid at all, and two adjacent tiles at different sample densities still line up.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTile.HeightAt(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the world height of one sample.

remarks.para: A sample is an offset from the level's terrain, not a world height. Terrain_GetZFromWorldCoordinates (igi2ed 0x632FF0) interpolates the four samples around a world position and adds ptTerrain->tPos.z to the result — the parent Terrain task's Z, not the tile's. The X and Y halves of the same function convert the query and the tile's own position into terrain space by subtracting the same origin from both, so those two cancel and only Z is left as a real offset.

Twenty-three of the twenty-four shipped levels author that Z as zero, which is why every path through here read the same either way. location1/level3 authors it as 36,864,000 — nine kilometres — and there the difference is the whole level: the ground draws nine kilometres below the buildings standing on it, which past a four-kilometre far plane is not a misplaced terrain but a black screen.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTile.PositionOf(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the world position of one sample.
member.returns: The position, with the sample's world height as Z.
member.exception: The sample is outside the tile.
member.remarks:
Samples sit at texel centres, not at grid corners. The tile spans centre ± worldExtent / 2 and is divided into texels, so sample i is at left + (i + 0.5) * texelWidth — which puts the first sample half a texel inside the edge and the last one half a texel short of the far edge.
That is the original's own arithmetic, read from both directions. TerrainMap_ResampleAndAlign (igi2.exe 0x571780) derives vBaseTexelWidth = vWorldWidth * 4096 / nWidth and snaps against tPos - (vWorldWidth * 4096 + vBaseTexelWidth) / 2, half a texel before the left edge; Terrain_SampleMaterial (0x56EDC0) inverts it as (x - centre + half) / texelWidth and rejects anything within half a texel of either edge.
Dividing by rather than Width - 1 is the part worth stating: a grid laid corner to corner would be one texel too wide and half a texel out of place, which reads as a terrain that almost lines up with the objects standing on it.

member.summary: Gets whether a world point is inside this tile, half a texel in from each edge.
member.param: The world X, in world units.
The world Y, in world units.
member.returns: when this tile answers for the point.

remarks.para: The test both of the sequel's height queries walk the tile list with — Terrain_VertexFunction (igi2 0x5706F0) and Terrain_GetZFromWorldCoordinates (igi2ed 0x632FF0) — and it is strict on all four sides and shrunk by half a texel, because a sample sits at its texel's centre and the outer half texel has no second sample to interpolate against.
Both walk the list backwards and take the first tile that contains the point, which is what makes a later-declared finer tile win over the coarse one it sits inside — the same priority draws with.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTile.IsSuperseded(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets whether a finer tile draws this square's ground in this tile's place.
member.param: How many samples across it is.
member.returns: when the square must not be drawn from this tile.

remarks.para: I.G.I. 2's tiles nest. A level lays a coarse map over the whole of itself and then finer maps over the parts that need them -- location1/level1's second tile is 512 metres of four-metre texels sitting inside two kilometres of thirty-two-metre ones -- and the ground under the finer map is drawn from the finer map alone.

Terrain_UpdateSubmaps (igi2ed 0x62C770) is where that is decided, once per load: for every cell of every mip of every map it walks the maps declared after it, keeps those whose texels are no larger than its own, and records the last one that contains the cell whole. TerrainRender_Draw reads that index at 0x668CBF and changes which map the square is reading rather than drawing the coarse one.

Drawing both is not a double cost but a visible fault: the passes blend SRCALPHA onto ONE, so a coarse tile left under a fine one adds a second ground to the frame -- pale sheets that cut through the hillsides wherever the two tessellations disagree.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTile.LightmapProjection
member.summary: Gets the planar projection that lays this tile's lightmap over the ground.
member.returns: A scale and an offset per axis: u = worldX * ScaleX + OffsetX.

remarks.para: The lightmap is a TEXTURE over the ground, not a colour on its vertices. TerrainRender_DrawRenderChunk_ (igi2ed 0x667400) draws the whole ground a second time for it: no material stream, the tile's TexInfo from TerrainContext_t::aptLightmap[i] on stage 0, TerrainRender_nLightmapVertexShader bound, and vertex-shader constants 11 and 12 loaded from ::atLightmapOffset[i] and ::atLightmapScale[i] — an affine projection of world XY, which is the pair this returns.

The projection is the tile's own extent, half a texel in on each side, because a lightmap texel answers for the same square a height sample does — the shipped maps are the same dimensions as their tile's height map, 128 by 128 beside 128 by 128.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTile.NormalAt(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Gets the surface normal at one sample, from the slope of the height map around it.

remarks.para: The original has no terrain normals to reproduce. Its ground is lit entirely by the per-sample lightmap the tile ships, carried in the vertex colour, and nothing in TerrainRender_CalculateRenderVertex (igi2ed 0x66A740) writes a normal at all. The remaster's deferred path needs one anyway: the sun, the ambient and the screen-space passes all ask the G-buffer which way a surface faces, and a ground that answers "up" everywhere is lit as a flat plate — which is what a hillside built out of thirty-two-metre texels looked like.

Central differences over the height map, which is the slope the ground actually has rather than the slope of whichever triangles the quadtree happened to emit. Taking it from the samples means a vertex keeps the same normal at every level of detail, so the ground does not re-light as it subdivides. Heights and texel sizes are both in world units, so the ratio is dimensionless.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainSurface
member.summary: An I.G.I. 2 level's ground: the tiles it declares, loaded and placed.

remarks.para: The level is the authority, not the archive. A level's TerrainMap tasks name the tiles it has, and the ids are sparse — location2/LEVEL6 declares only tile 2. Enumerating heightmaps.res instead would load four tiles that belong to no level at all, because location3/LEVEL4 ships two while declaring none.

A tile missing any of its three files is complete rather than broken, which is the original's own tolerance: TerrainMap_Alloc substitutes a zeroed material map and a white lightmap and carries on. The height map is the one that cannot be substituted usefully, so a tile without it is skipped.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainTessellation
member.summary: One frame's worth of ground for a tile, and what the quadtree did to produce it.
member.param: The geometry, in the same shape a full-detail build produces.
How many quadtree leaves were emitted.
How many squares the clipping planes rejected, subtrees included.
How many squares came off the traversal stack.

The emitted leaves' areas added up, in samples squared. The traversal only ever divides a square into four equal quadrants, so this plus equalling the root's own area is a proof that the leaves tile it exactly — no gap, no overlap — which is the property a level-of-detail mesh most easily loses.
The area a finer tile draws instead, which this one left alone. Zero for a level whose tiles do not nest, and for the finest tile of one whose tiles do.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainVertex
member.summary: The ground at a point, Terrain_VertexFunction (igi2 0x5706F0), with the arithmetic the client's FPU performs.

remarks.para: The point is relative to the terrain, as single floats. The finest tile that holds it, half a texel in from its edges, answers; the first tile answers for anything else. The point becomes a fractional sample index, clamped to the grid, and the height is interpolated over whichever of the cell's two triangles holds it, with that triangle's normal.

The material is the corner material when all four agree. Where three agree it splits the cell along a diagonal; otherwise it is the nearest corner's. The light is the nearest lightmap texel's average channel, scaled so that 255 reads as two. A tile with no lightmap file was given a white one when it loaded.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainView
member.summary: Where the ground is being looked at from, and the half-spaces it may be culled against.

remarks.para: All four planes pass through the eye. That is the shape TerrainRender_SetupClippingPlanes (igi2ed 0x6681A0) builds when no clip window is active: it zeroes each plane's point, fills in the four side normals from the projection's tan half-angles, rotates them by the inverted view rotation and then subtracts tDisplacement — which puts every point at the camera. A plane is stored as a point followed by a normal, and TerrainRender_IsSquareOutOfSight (0x66AE50) treats dot(p - point, normal) > 0 as outside.
The original's other branch, taken when a clip window is set, copies arbitrary points and normals out of Clipping_GetClipPlanes. That path belongs to the editor's split views and is not reproduced.
There is no near or far plane in the set — four side planes only. Distance is what the detail test is for.

member.param: The eye position, in world units.

member.summary: Gets the eye position, in world units.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainView.PlaneNormals
member.summary: Gets the outward normals of the culling half-spaces, all through .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2TerrainView.FromCamera(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Camera3D@,System.Single,System.Single)
member.summary: Builds the view one frame is drawn from.
member.param: The eye and its orientation, in the height field's units.
The vertical field of view, in radians.
member.returns: The view, with the frustum's four side planes.

remarks.para: The four normals are the original's, in view space: (-1, 0, -tanX), (1, 0, -tanX), (0, -1, -tanY) and (0, 1, -tanY), each normalised — left, right, bottom and top of a frustum whose apex is the eye. They are then rotated into world space by the camera's orientation, which is what TerrainRender_SetupClippingPlanes does with the inverted view rotation.

One difference, stated rather than copied: the original normalises the top plane's Y component with 1 / sqrt(tanY * tanX + 1) where every other component uses 1 / sqrt(tanY * tanY + 1) (0x6681A0, the store to flt_85233C8). That mixes the two half-angles and leaves the normal non-unit whenever the aspect ratio is not one. It looks like a typo in the original and it only ever loosens the cull, so the port uses the consistent form.
A camera with a degenerate orientation — a default-constructed one, as a test may pass — yields zero normals, which reject nothing. That is the safe direction to fail in.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2Train
member.summary: A locomotive and the carriages behind it, placed along the spline they ride.

remarks.para: A train has no position. Its Position parameter is a single Real32 — a distance along the spline its RailroadQTaskID names — and everything else follows from walking that curve. The carriages are child Train tasks and carry no distance of their own: each hangs one carriage-length behind the one in front.

A carriage's length is not authored either. Train_UpdateInternalDataHandler (igi2ed 0x47F8E0) measures it as the distance between the model's first two magic vertices, which are its couplings. That is the only reason this needs the models at all, and the reason a world walk given none places no trains.

Only the locomotive moves. That handler calls Train_Move (0x47F9D0) only when the task's parent is not itself a Train, and Train_Move then places the whole rake: Train_GetPositions (0x47FA70) walks one coupling point per carriage and Train_MoveCarriage (0x47FB20) turns each carriage to span the two points it sits between. Every step uses the LOCOMOTIVE's Flip Direction, not each carriage's own.

member.summary: Builds the rotation a carriage takes from the two couplings it spans.
member.param: The forward coupling, which is where the carriage stands.

member.remarks: Train_MoveCarriage builds it from the chord alone, not from the curve: the carriage points at the coupling ahead of it however the track bends in between, which is what a rigid carriage does. The side axis starts horizontal, so a carriage rolls only where the track is banked. Two couplings at the same point leave it unturned.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2Water
member.summary: I.G.I. 2's water module, h/2/water.c: every body of water a level makes (Water_ptQTaskList, in the order they are made), the questions asked of them — how deep a point lies (Water_IsUnderWater) — and the ripples and splashes that steps, bullets and blasts leave on them.

remarks.para: The surface is logic, not only looks: its height under a point is the sum of its layers' sine trains and of the ripples still spreading over it (), and that height decides whether a human wades, swims or stands dry. The layers move with the flow's clock (Water_vTime, a sixtieth of a second a flow tick).

The module keeps its own random stream (Water_tRandomState), seeded once as the module opens, which only a blast's spray draws from; and two throttles shared by every body, one for the ripples of a wading human and one for those of bullets.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterSurface
member.summary: The water a level places: where each sheet is, and what animates it.

remarks.para: A sheet is a Water task with WaterLayer children, each layer one travelling wave train. Water_SetVertexFunctionParameters (igi2ed 0x6474A0) collects them and stops at four — a fifth layer is authored data the engine never reads. It also fixes the clock: Water_vTime = Timer_nTicks / 60, so wave phase is seconds at the simulation's own tick rate.

The displacement is in , and an earlier version of this remark was wrong about it. It said the waves were evaluated by a compiled vertex shader and could not be recovered. They are not: Water_VertexFunction (igi2ed 0x645B30) sums the trains on the CPU and differences the normal, and Water_EnterHandler hands a pointer to it into the renderer's draw method as a callback. The name of Water_SetVertexFunctionParameters is what misled — those are arguments to an ordinary function.

How a sheet blends is readable, and it is not what one would guess. WaterRender_SetBlendState (0x57B6F0) always enables blending and then branches on WaterRender_iQualityLevel: above zero it sets SRCBLEND = ONE with DESTBLEND = SRCALPHA, so the water's own colour is added whole and the scene behind it is attenuated by the water's alpha; at zero or below it falls back to ordinary SRCALPHA/INVSRCALPHA. The two are visibly different, and only the second is the blend a port would arrive at on its own.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveTrain
member.summary: One wave train, in the form the surface is actually evaluated in.
member.param: The east component of the direction the train travels.
Radians of phase per engine unit travelled.
How far the crest rises, in engine units.
member.remarks:
Derived from a WaterLayer's four authored parameters by WaterLayer_UpdateInternalDataHandler (igi2ed 0x647750), which is five lines long and settles every one of them:
[19] = sin(Angle * 0.017453292) // the direction pair, from degrees [20] = cos(Angle * 0.017453292) [13] = 6.2831855 / (Frequency * 4096) // so "Frequency" is a wavelength, in metres [14] = Amplitude * 4096 // metres to engine units
The one that matters is [13]. Frequency is the parameter's name and a wavelength is what it holds — the engine divides by it. A reader that took the name at face value would get the sea inside out, with the short waves long and the long ones short.
The direction pair is (sin, cos) and not the other way round, so a zero angle travels along +Y — a compass bearing, matching the camera's own zero heading.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField
member.summary: The height and the normal of a water sheet: a sum of sine trains, evaluated per vertex.

remarks.para: This corrects an earlier claim of this port's, which said the displacement was locked inside a compiled vertex shader and could not be recovered. It is not: Water_VertexFunction (igi2ed 0x645B30) sums the trains on the CPU and builds the normal by finite difference. The misreading came from the name of Water_SetVertexFunctionParameters — those parameters are arguments to an ordinary function, and Water_EnterHandler passes a pointer to it into the renderer's draw method as a callback. What is a shader is the reflection lookup, which is a separate question.
The whole surface, then:
remarks.code: z(x, y, t) = Σ sin((x·dirX + y·dirY + phase)·spatialFreq + t·speed) · amplitude · attenuation
remarks.para: with x and y measured from the sheet's own centre — Water_IsUnderWater (0x6477D0) subtracts the sheet's position before calling, and the height that comes back is relative to the sheet too.

Two sheet-wide constants come out of Water_UpdateInternalDataHandler's last three lines (0x6460B0): the phase is Size × 8192, which is twice the sheet's radius in engine units and is there to keep the sine's argument positive right across a sheet that spans ±radius; and the attenuation divisor is Fadeout / 4096, so amplitude falls away as 1 / max(1, metres from centre × Fadeout) and the far edge of a large sheet lies flatter than its middle.

Not reproduced: the ripples. Water_VertexFunction also walks a vector of transient disturbances — a raised cosine of (1 - cos((d - inner)·2π / 2·width)) × amplitude inside an annulus — which Water_GunShotEffect and the physics hit handler push into. Those are runtime events rather than level data, and belong with whatever drives them.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField.PhaseScale
member.summary: How the sheet's Size becomes the phase added to every sample.
member.remarks: water[216] = Size * 8192 — twice the radius, in engine units.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField.AttenuationScale
member.summary: How the sheet's Fadeout becomes the attenuation divisor.
member.remarks: water[220] = Fadeout * 0.00024414062, which is a division by 4,096.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField.SampleScale
member.summary: What fraction of the mean wavelength the finite difference steps by.
member.remarks: Water_SetVertexFunctionParameters sets sampleScale = 40.959999 / layers × Σ Frequency, which is 40.96 × the mean wavelength in metres — and since a metre is 4,096 units, exactly a hundredth of the mean wavelength. A step tied to the waves it measures rather than a fixed epsilon, which is what keeps the normal meaningful across sheets whose wavelengths differ by two orders of magnitude.

How far the point is from the centre, which attenuates the waves. Zero leaves them at full height, which is what Water_IsUnderWater passes — it wants the surface, not a fade.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField.AttenuationAt(System.Single)
member.summary: Gets how much a train's amplitude survives at one distance from the centre.
member.remarks: 1 / max(1, radius × Fadeout / 4096). The clamp is upward, on the divisor, so inside the first metre — and whenever Fadeout is nought — the waves are at full height rather than unbounded.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WaterWaveField.NormalAt(System.Single,System.Single,System.Double,System.Single)
member.summary: Gets the surface normal at a point on the sheet.
member.param: How far east of the sheet's centre, in engine units.
How far the point is from the centre.
member.returns: The unit normal, pointing up out of the water.
member.remarks: A forward difference, not an analytic derivative, because that is what the original does: it samples the height at the point, at one east and at one north, and takes (-s·dzEast, -s·dzNorth, s²) normalised — the cross product of the two tangents. The third component being positive is one more confirmation that Z is up.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WorldBuilder
member.summary: Walks an I.G.I. 2 level into placements.

remarks.para: Three things the first game's walk does not do, and all three are why this is a seam rather than a parameter.

item.description: Models resolve through a table over every open pack, in load order. Game_CreateHandler (igi2ed 0x4469A0) opens common, then new, then the location's, then the level's — and MTP_VirModel_GetPtr (0x41EED0) returns the first match walking from the head, so common shadows the level. That is the opposite of the first game, where the level pack is opened second and wins.
Lightmaps bind by task id, out of the level's own archive, rather than by placement.

Characters are skipped, because their model is a character kind drawn by a character presenter on a schedule the world pass does not own — the same division the first game draws under, reached from a different set of type names.

remarks.para: The fifth MTP_Load in that handler is the editor pack, loaded from LOCAL:editor/ under a "Loading editor..." caption. It is the editor's own and no part of the game, which is why four is the number here and not five.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2Placement
member.summary: One model a level places in the world, with everything needed to draw it.
member.param: The level task id the placement was declared with, or when it has none. This is what names its baked lightmaps — see .
The task type that placed it, kept for diagnostics rather than for drawing.
The model's base name, without a level-of-detail suffix or an extension.
Where it stands, in engine units.

Its orientation as the three angles level data stores, in radians. Real32x9 is the declared type and a nine-float matrix is what the engine keeps, but what a script writes is three angles — see ScriptArgumentReader.ReadReal32x9.
Which of the frame's sixteen call queues it is drawn in. Zero for the task types that declare no group, which is also the queue an object lands in when a level does not say.

A second model this one carries, which sits on the host's first magic vertex rather than at a position of its own — a security camera's body on its bracket, a gun's barrel on its mount. Empty for the great majority of placements, which carry nothing.
The mounted model's own facing, in the same three angles, already composed with the host's.
The orientation given as a matrix rather than as three angles, for a type whose handler builds one directly. Null for everything placed at an authored facing, which is nearly everything.

How the placement's geometry is derived, for the few types that deform their model rather than draw it as it ships — a wire stretched down its span, a spline segment bent along its curve. Null for everything drawn as authored, which is nearly everything.
The model the object wears once destroyed, its Destroyed model, or empty for a type that has none: what an ExplodeObject swaps to when it explodes (ExplodeObject_SetExploded, igi2 0x49D010).

Which of the owning task's model SLOTS this is wearing, counted from one, or zero when the type has a single slot or the port has not established its enumeration. It is the group letter in the name of the object's baked lightmap — LightmapInfo_AddLightmapVirModelToEnumeration (igi2 0x53C920) writes acIndexLetters[nModelVariation], and a slot's variation is its index plus one — so it is what picks the matching bake out of the level's archive. See .
The magic task type of the attach point hangs on, or empty when it hangs on this model; see .
The models the object may wear by its state, a switch's five (), or for an object with one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WorldScene
member.summary: Everything an I.G.I. 2 level places in the world, walked out of its task tree.

remarks.para: Read by parameter name, not by task class. Twenty-three of the sequel's task types carry a Model, from EditRigidObj through Door, Lift, Car and Fence to Terminal, and every one of them declares the model, the position and the orientation under the same three names. Walking the names collects all twenty-three at once and needs no class for any of them, which is what makes a world drawable long before the gameplay behind it exists.

Only — and a typed task that says it is placed () — is walked, and that is the rule rather than a limitation: a type with a class has a subsystem that owns it, and a forest or a terrain tile is not one model at one place. When a gameplay class arrives for a type that is currently a placeholder, its objects leave this scene and become that subsystem's business — which is the correct direction, because by then something knows how to animate them.
This is geometry, not gameplay. It carries no collision, no visibility set and no lightmap binding; those come later, from the level's .mtp packs and its object lightmaps.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WorldScene.Bindings
member.summary: The types that name their model, position or facing something other than the usual.

remarks.para: Every entry is the rest transform its create handler builds, read out of the dedicated server's igi2.exe rather than inferred from the parameter names:

item.description: Door — Door_UpdateInternalDataHandler (0x537E10) copies the task's position into tOriginalPosStart, sets isClosed, and calls Door_SetPosition (0x5362B0), which offsets by stop × slider and turns by maxAngle × slider. A closed door has a slider of zero, so it stands exactly at Position start under Orientation. 802 of them in the corpus.
Switch — Switch_SetModel (0x4DA360) indexes the five models as on, on-pressed, off, off-pressed, destroyed. Unpressed and undamaged, Initial on alone chooses between the first and the third.

SCamera — SCamera_UpdateInternalDataHandler (0x48FB80) builds the holder's rotation from a single angle's sine and cosine, so the bracket turns about the up axis only. The camera body is a separate child task whose own handler (0x48F370) places it on a MAGIC VERTEX of the holder, which is why only the holder is bound here.

StationaryGun, AIStationaryGunHolder — AIStationaryGunHolder_UpdateInternalDataHandler copies the parameter block's orientation straight into the model object. An automatic gun's barrel is an object of its gun's own, the attach point of type AIStationaryGun: AIStationaryGun_UpdateInternalDataHandler makes it a child of that attach object, on its first magic vertex, so it is walked after it.

Wire — Wire_UpdateInternalDataHandler (0x49B720) gives the model no position of its own. It puts it at the midpoint of Start position and Stop position, builds an orientation whose middle column is the direction down the span, and scales the model's local Y by length × 0.000244140625 — one over WORLD_METER. So a wire is bound by its endpoints rather than by the usual parameter names; see .

SplineObjWaypoint — the waypoint itself is a RigidDynCubeObj whose model is its Waypoint Model: SplineObjWaypoint_CreateHandler (0x641250) passes that parameter to MTP_GetLODVirModelExists and hands the result to RigidDynCubeObj_Init, so a waypoint naming a model the installation does not ship is created with none and draws nothing. 584 of the corpus's 713 name ai-arrow, which is that case — no file of that name exists anywhere in the retail data, and the level scripts are the only thing that mention it. The other 94 name a real model and are drawn. Its Orientation is a Real32x9, which level data stores as the same three Euler angles every other type's is.

Lift — the authored start. Lift_SetPositionToFirstFloor (0x46DD50) moves a lift onto its first Floor child at load, which this does not do; the eight lifts in the corpus stand where the editor left them until it does.

remarks.para: Not here, and why. A SplineObjWaypoint's Segment Model is swept along the spline between consecutive waypoints rather than placed at either, so it is read from the run as a whole — see . RotateAttachment (250) has no position at all — it hangs off its parent. Train (9) rides a spline. ComputerHilight (108) names MARKER_NONE, a sentinel for the computer overlay rather than a model, and LevelInfo (19) names a script path. Each is a subsystem, not a name.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WorldScene.CharacterTypes
member.summary: The task types whose Model is not a file name.

remarks.para: Measured, not assumed. Across the 24 shipped levels the static props resolve by file name almost perfectly — Fence, Ladder, Cabinet, Car and ConveyorBelt at 100%, EditRigidObj at 8,296 of 8,469 — while these do not: HumanSoldier resolves 34 of 901, HumanPlayer none of 19, and EditBoneObj 90 of 301.

So a character's Model is a character kind that something else turns into geometry, not a file: level 1 asks for rsg1_1, rsg2_1 and rsg3_1 where the archives hold only rsg_1 through rsg_4, which are its levels of detail. Which table performs that lookup is the first question M2-4 has to answer, and the .mtp packs each level ships beside its models are the place to look.
A world renderer skips these: a character is drawn by a character presenter, from a skinned mesh, on a schedule the world pass does not own.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.Igi2WorldScene.ModelResourceName(System.String)
member.summary: Gets the resource name a model is loaded under.
member.param: The model as level data names it.
member.remarks: The name is used as it is written. Level data already carries the level-of-detail suffix — it asks for 940_07_1, not 940_07 — so a renderer that appended one would ask for 940_07_1_1 and find nothing. Which is exactly what this method did when it was first written: every one of the corpus's models failed to resolve, all at once, which is the good way for that mistake to show up.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.IIgi2PlacementGeometry
member.summary: How a placement's geometry is derived, when it is not the model as it was authored.

remarks.para: Most of the sequel's objects are a model placed at a position under an orientation, and the renderer draws the shipped mesh unchanged. A few are not: a Wire stretches its model down the span it is strung across, and a SplineObjSegment bends its model along a curve. Both deform the vertices before they reach the vertex buffer — the original does it every frame in Direct3DRender_ProcessVerticesSplineRigid and its siblings — and both therefore need geometry of their own rather than the model's.
This is the seam that keeps that out of the world walk. A placement says how its geometry is made; the drawable scene, which is the only stage holding a , asks it to make one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.TerrainMapTask
member.summary: One tile of terrain — I.G.I. 2's TerrainMap: where a tile sits, how large it is, and the id that names its height, material and lightmap files.

remarks.para: The eight parameters land one for one on TerrainMap_t's edit fields in igi2.exe, in declaration order: iID, nEditWidth, nEditHeight, tEditPos, vEditWorldWidth, vEditWorldHeight, vSoftenEdgeSize, zDEMFile. The engine copies each edit field to its run-time twin on load, which is why the declaration names the edit half and the loader validates against it.

The map extent and the world extent are independent. counts samples and measures distance, so the sample spacing is the ratio of the two — a tile can be resampled without moving, which is exactly what TerrainMap_ResampleAndAlign does. and are also the numbers each of the three files is checked against as it loads: a file whose header disagrees is rejected outright rather than stretched.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.TerrainMaterialTask
member.summary: One row of a level's terrain material table — I.G.I. 2's TerrainMaterial, selected per sample by a tile's .tmm map.

remarks.para: The seven parameters land on TerrainMaterial_t in igi2.exe: iID, iGameMaterial, then atTexture[0] and atTexture[1] — a two-element array of TerrainTexture_t, each a filename and a scale — and finally eMappingStyle. The declaration interleaves the array differently from the struct, naming both filenames and then both scales, which is why the two are read as four separate parameters rather than as a pair of rows.

is the value a .tmm sample carries, not the task's position in the tree, so the table is sparse by design and a level may declare its materials in any order. Across the retail tree the sample values span 0 to 7.

This replaces I.G.I. 1's arrangement rather than extending it: there, the game material came from a per-face selector inside the terrain's own TAMC table, and the texture came from a texture modifier bound to a chunk. Here one row carries both, and a sample picks the row directly.

member.summary: A level's terrain root — I.G.I. 2's Terrain, the task every and hangs under.

remarks.para: The fourteen parameters are the ones the retail levels declare, in that order; 22 of the 24 shipped levels declare this type, so registering the class turns every one of them into a check on these attributes. Each maps to a named field of Terrain_t in igi2.exe, which is what settles what they mean:

item.description: editor state: the height brush, the shadow sampler, and the random generator.

remarks.para: Two thirds of the block is editor-only. vBrushSize, vBrushPower, the four vGenerator* fields and nNumShadowSamples/vShadowSpread drive the terrain editor's brush and its lightmap bake; nothing reads them while a mission is being played. They are carried anyway because the declaration carries them and the arity has to match — dropping one would silently shift every parameter after it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.WaterLayerTask
member.summary: One wave train on a body of water — I.G.I. 2's WaterLayer, a child of a .

remarks.para: A directional sine: a frequency, an amplitude, a speed and a heading. The surface is the sum of its water's layers, which is how a sheet gets a swell and a chop at once without either being modelled — WaterLayer_t carries a precomputed tRotation beside the angle, so the heading is resolved once and the per-vertex work is a dot product and a sine.
Four parameters, and none of them are editor state. This is one of the few I.G.I. 2 task types that is nothing but level data.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.WaterTask
member.summary: A body of water — I.G.I. 2's Water: one horizontal sheet, its surface material, and the environment cube maps it reflects.

remarks.para: Thirty parameters, and they divide sharply. The first dozen describe the water itself: where the sheet sits, how big it is, how it is tessellated, and the optical properties WaterRender shades it with — and are a depth-absorption term and a Fresnel cutoff, not decoration. The waves themselves are not here: they are the children, summed.

Everything from onward is the environment map and how it was baked. The camera position, orientation and field of view, and the five booleans naming which kinds of task to draw, are the editor's capture settings — Envmap_CubeMapRender (igi2ed 0x581930) runs six renders with them. They are recorded in the level so a map can be rebuilt, and are not consulted while a mission is played; what is consulted is the baked result, named through .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.WaterTask.CubeMapFaceResource(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds the resource name of one face of one of this water's environment maps.
member.exception: The face is not one of the six.
The task holds no level id.
member.remarks: cubemap_<waterTaskId>_<index:000>_<face>.bmp. The task id is , the same level-table slot that names a forest's placement file, so a water's baked maps are also named by where the level put the task rather than by a parameter. The face number is the D3DCUBEMAP_FACES index it is loaded into, in order: the original passes the array straight through, face i from file i.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi2.World.WindTask
member.summary: The level's wind — I.G.I. 2's Wind, which drives the vertex morph that makes foliage move.

remarks.para: A single oscillator, not a field: one constant strength plus a main sine and a clamped gust sine, blowing in one direction for the whole level. A says how many of its model's levels of detail respond to it, and Phase shift between morph channels is what stops every tree in a stand swaying in unison.

17 of the 24 shipped levels declare it, so wind is per level and optional. It is one of the seven task types the sequel adds outright — I.G.I. 1 has no counterpart, because it has no foliage that moves.
